analysis.body:
Federal agencies are experimenting with AI across a growing portfolio of use cases, though most remain in early stages. According to the GAO, twenty of twenty-three agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, with agency reported uses including analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases. However, most of these reported AI use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production, with about 200 instances where agencies reported currently using AI. This early adoption posture reflects both interest and caution as government technology infrastructure scales to support operational deployment.

Data quality problems are slowing federal AI management. The GAO's analysis of agencies' inventories of use cases identified instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, with five agencies providing comprehensive information while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Some inventories did not include required data elements such as the AI life cycle stage or an indication of whether an AI use case was releasable or not. Additionally, two inventories included AI uses that were later determined by the agencies to not be AI. Without accurate inventories, according to the GAO, the government's management of its use of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

Implementation of federal AI policy is uneven across agencies and requirements. The GAO found that ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt from the requirements. The Department of Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements—Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence—while the Offices of Management and Budget and Personnel Management did not fully implement selected requirements. OMB has not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and OPM has not yet established or updated an occupational category for those employees performing AI work.

The regulatory and policy infrastructure is building but incomplete. Federal law and guidance have several requirements for agencies implementing AI, but they haven't all been met. According to the GAO, there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, meaning agencies cannot consistently manage AI. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling sustained commitment, yet without consistent acquisition guidance and risk management frameworks in place, agencies cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits at scale. The Stanford HAI's AI Index identifies a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with data transparency declining even as adoption spreads globally.

Policymakers are responding through legislation and international coordination. As tracked on this site's AI Laws section, 5,856 AI bills are tracked across 53 jurisdictions and updated daily, reflecting intense legislative activity at the state and federal level. Internationally, the OECD.AI policy observatory monitors over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, and the GPAI initiative joined forces with OECD member countries' work on AI to create an integrated partnership, while organizations developing advanced AI systems can submit reports to facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. Government agencies preparing to deploy AI should expect an evolving compliance landscape and should prioritize accurate inventory practices and risk assessment frameworks as foundational work, regardless of use case.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page tracks artificial-intelligence legislation across the United States, listing every bill by state. It reports that 5,560 AI bills are monitored in 53 jurisdictions, with updates made daily from LegiScan. The site also references a series of books and audit tools, but the primary focus is on the legislative tracking.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
